stories.title: 3verest uses Equinix to build sovereign AI for healthcare
stories.summary: Healthcare providers will be able to keep scans, prompts and AI inference inside national borders as 3verest expands sovereign cloud controls.
stories.content:
# 3verest uses Equinix to build sovereign AI for healthcare

Tue, 25th Aug 2026 (Yesterday)

3verest is using Equinix Fabric Geo Zones to build sovereign AI infrastructure for healthcare organisations, aiming to keep medical imaging data and related AI activity within national borders.

The arrangement extends 3verest's approach beyond data storage to the broader flow of AI workloads. It is intended to help hospitals, medical imaging providers, healthcare technology vendors and government health bodies keep AI inference, prompts and network traffic within the relevant jurisdiction.

The issue is becoming more pressing as healthcare providers use AI tools to analyse scans and other clinical information. In regulated sectors, providers must account not only for where records are stored, but also where models process requests and how traffic moves across networks.

3verest operates a healthcare cloud focused on sovereign deployments across Australia, the UK, Germany, the US, Canada and the European Union. Its platform supports more than 200 customers across 21 markets, with sovereign points of presence in Australia, the UK, the US, Canada and the European Union.

Equinix Fabric Geo Zones is designed to enforce geographic restrictions at the network layer between clouds and providers. This allows network traffic to remain within approved boundaries even during failover or rerouting, which can create compliance concerns when data paths change unexpectedly.

For healthcare groups handling imaging and clinical data, that distinction matters because a sovereign cloud setup can be undermined if related AI requests or interconnection traffic cross a border. The model is intended to preserve jurisdictional control across the full AI workflow, not only at the point of storage.

### Platform buildout

As part of that expansion, 3verest is developing several healthcare AI products. These include Bifrost, a sovereign AI environment for healthcare; Forge, a developer platform for radiology vendors, AI developers and healthcare organisations; and Heimdall, a control layer between healthcare applications and AI models.

Heimdall is intended to route prompts, apply guardrails and direct requests to the appropriate models while keeping data within a defined boundary. Forge is built on Firecracker micro-VM technology, while Bifrost combines GPU infrastructure, retrieval-augmented generation, AI models and managed AI services for healthcare use cases.

Scott Crawford, Founder and Chief Executive Officer at 3verest, outlined the company's view of the compliance shift created by AI.

"Healthcare doesn't need another cloud. It needs infrastructure built around sovereignty from the ground up. The industry has spent years asking where data is stored, but AI changes the question to where intelligence runs. Patient imaging, clinical prompts, and AI inference must remain inside the jurisdiction, not just the archive. Equinix gives us the global digital infrastructure to build sovereign healthcare clouds consistently across multiple countries, while Fabric Geo Zones extends those guarantees to the network itself. That means our customers can adopt AI with confidence, knowing sovereignty is designed into every layer of the platform, not added afterwards," Crawford said.

### Broader question

Equinix said the same network control principle applies beyond healthcare to other regulated industries. It argued that sovereignty can no longer be treated as a setting within one cloud provider when applications and AI systems are distributed across multiple environments.

Arun Dev, Vice President of Digital Interconnection at Equinix, said: "AI is fundamentally changing what sovereignty means. Organisations must now govern not only where data is stored, but how it moves between clouds, applications, and AI services. Sovereignty cannot be a setting inside a single cloud. It must be enforced at the network layer across every provider and every connection. That's exactly what Fabric Geo Zones delivers. 3verest demonstrates how healthcare organisations can embrace sovereign AI while maintaining the security, compliance and operational resilience required for highly regulated clinical environments. The same principle applies to other sovereignty-critical sectors, including financial services, where data control, regulatory compliance and operational continuity are equally non-negotiable."

Equinix operates more than 280 IBX data centres across 77 metropolitan areas in 36 countries. Fabric Geo Zones is available in markets including Australia, Brazil, Canada, Japan, Switzerland, the UK, the US and the European Union.

Through that footprint, 3verest can privately interconnect with healthcare providers, original equipment manufacturer partners and cloud services while maintaining jurisdictional controls over sensitive healthcare data, the companies said.

stories.title: Data Center Construction at Midyear: Demand, Friction, and Building Discipline
stories.summary: Data center buildouts are booming in 2026, but challenges like power, labor, and community concerns demand innovation and collaboration.
stories.content:
Data center buildouts are booming in 2026, but challenges like power, labor, and community concerns demand innovation and collaboration.

August 24, 2026

Data center construction remains the defining infrastructure story of 2026. In a broader construction market showing signs of softness, digital infrastructure is a robust exception. Citing the Dodge Momentum Index, Construction Dive reported that data center construction planning momentum picked up in July, “again shining as the brightest sector in building.”

This pipeline reflects demand for insurance and risk management expertise in technically complex, capital-intensive projects. Zurich’s global construction insurance business recorded 18% growth in the first half of 2026, and since Zurich launched a specialized Data Center Project Guard offering in January, our construction team has received more than three dozen broker submissions representing approximately $140 billion in project value. This is a powerful signal of demand, but demand is not the same as delivery. Friction is increasing, and it is instructive. Friction is a call and an opportunity to innovate, collaborate and communicate.

In the second half of the year, the question is how the technology, construction and insurance industries can deliver on the demand for data center capacity safely, sustainably and with the support of the communities where these projects are slated. The same issues surfaced repeatedly at construction and insurance industry events this summer: power constraints, workforce shortages, insurance capacity, and community concerns chief among them.

## Community Concerns Over Data Center Expansion

While energy and labor challenges have been a topic from the start, community concern over data centers has heated up this summer.

In July, New York became the first state to impose a one-year pause on new hyperscale data centers while the state develops standards intended to protect ratepayers, the energy grid, the environment and local communities. In Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott ordered audits of data center projects seeking grid connection, citing concerns about electricity demand, water use, local impacts, and project transparency.

Dynamics like these are not being dismissed by any of the data center stakeholders in our orbit, whether hyperscalers, co-locators or general contractors. Communities are asking legitimate questions about energy costs, environmental impacts, and long-term accountability.

In the rush to meet the need for digital infrastructure to support advanced AI and society’s growing expectations for financial, healthcare, and entertainment services, these questions must still be addressed. That requires a collaborative approach.

In a recent Fortune commentary, Chris Crosby, CEO of Compass Datacenters, made the point that communities need better partners, not blanket bans, and that trust must be earned through transparency, regular communication and commitments residents can see over time. He outlined five questions that every data center developer should address for the community. That is a constructive way to frame the challenge.

## Balancing Growth and Community Expectations

From an insurance and risk engineering perspective, the industry is seeing early signs of progress on the challenges. An encouraging development is that data center owners are increasingly bringing insurers into projects earlier, often before final site selection or design decisions are made. By adopting a holistic, lifecycle perspective, insurers and owners can collaborate to identify risks that may not be significant during construction but could become critical over decades of operation.

That broader perspective is increasingly important as campuses grow larger and more complex, driven by the need for more computing power in one place to improve AI training and inference performance.

When engaged early, insurance underwriting and risk engineering teams can help surface issues before they become costly problems. Early plan review can help owners address protection systems and engineering requirements up front to support longer-term insurability. Resolving these matters earlier can be pivotal to securing ongoing property insurance on terms and at pricing the owner would prefer.

## Collaborative Solutions

Power specialists in our risk engineering group point out that the discussion on energy sourcing is rapidly evolving. It’s no longer only about whether enough electricity can be generated from the grid for the data center. It is about whether high-quality, reliable power can be delivered when it is needed to all who depend on it, including homes and businesses.

Data center developers are evaluating multiple pathways to alleviate strain on the electrical grid, including natural gas microgrids, fuel cells, battery energy storage systems, geothermal and, over a longer time horizon, nuclear. Many are committed to paying for their additional usage in one way or another.

We are still a long way from fit-out, as the industry navigates the challenges of this unprecedented buildout to support the AI revolution. But foundations are being laid. The data center buildout has only just begun, but is already entering a more disciplined, collaborative phase.

stories.title: AEMO predicts seven-fold rise in data centre power use over next decade
stories.summary: Scales up forecast.
stories.content:
## Key points

- AEMO forecasts data centre electricity consumption will grow seven-fold over the next decade, from 5 TWh currently to around 34 TWh.
- The 2026 forecast is based on 225 known data centre projects, though more than 40 percent since 2025 have dropped out or regressed in connection status.
- New standards for energy and water consumption by data centres could be agreed federally as early as Wednesday, though state sign-up remains unclear.

The Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) is predicting a seven-fold increase in electricity consumption by data centres over the next decade.

In its latest electricity statement of expectations [pdf], the public utility organisation projected growth “from current levels of 5 terawatt hours (TWh) to around 34 TWh”.

In last year’s forecast, its forecast for data centre electricity consumption was “21.4 TWh by 2034-35 and 35.7 TWh by 2054-55.”

“Rapid growth in data centres, driven by increased artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and cloud services, remains one of the most significant sources of forecast growth and uncertainty as a strong pipeline of projects is evident in grid connection enquiries,” AEMO said.

“Data centres are expected to become an increasingly significant driver of electricity demand over the medium and long term, particularly in NSW and Victoria where the concentration of development is projected to be greatest.”

AEMO said its 2026 forecast is based on “the potential development of 225 known data centre projects”.

However, it noted there is significant uncertainty, with proposed data centre projects often not reaching build status.

“More than 40 percent of data centre projects since 2025 [have] either dropped out or regressed in connection status,” it noted.

“Data centre operators [also] often indicate that new facilities may take five-to-10 years to reach capacity.

“Consistent with international experience , mature data centres in aggregate are projected to utilise around 50 percent of their network connection capacity, and operate constantly with only minor increases in consumption during working hours, relative to non-working hours.”

This year, AEMO also modelled the potential impact on the electricity grid if data centre growth in demand was realised up to four years sooner; the results, it said, showed grid reliability could be maintained.

It noted the importance of doing the modelling, given the growth in data centre proposals generally.

New standards for energy and water consumption by data centres could be agreed at a federal level as early as Wednesday, *the ABC* has reported, although it’s unclear if states will sign up.

stories.title: Prometheus’ 1.5 GW Texas Data Center Plan Tests Private Power
stories.summary: The developer plans an islanded campus with onsite generation, but reaching its 2027 target will require a customer, modular construction, and a new power plant.
stories.content:
The developer plans an islanded campus with onsite generation, but reaching its 2027 target will require a customer, modular construction, and a new power plant.

Data center developer Prometheus Hyperscale is betting that the fastest way to put AI compute in West Texas is to avoid an initial ERCOT grid connection altogether.

The company plans a 1.5 GW data center campus in Pecos, Texas, powered by an islanded generation system. The project has a development path to 2.5 GW, with pipeline natural gas supplying the initial generation and a planned co-located fractionation facility providing ethane fuel flexibility after it enters service.

That approach removes the campus from the initial ERCOT interconnection process, but it does not remove the difficult work of supplying power. Prometheus and its eventual customer will need to manage generation, firm fuel supplies, air permitting, maintenance, redundancy, and financing – responsibilities typically handled by a utility in a grid-connected project.

Adam Mirick, Prometheus’ chief energy and business officer, told Data Center Knowledge in an interview that the company has already spoken with several prospective customers.

The project, however, remains contingent on a customer commitment. Prometheus says a modular deployment could deliver 100-150 MW of compute capacity in 2027.

“If we had a commitment, I’d say in October, perhaps we can bring on 100 to 150 megawatts of compute in 2027,” Mirick said. “It’s very challenging to bring anything to market in ’27 right now between the generation, between the MDCs, the contractors, all of it.”

## A Power Plant Behind the Data Center

The 1.5 GW figure represents planned IT load, not generation capacity. Prometheus favors rich-burn reciprocating engines for the initial generation blocks because they can be deployed incrementally and accommodate fuel variability. Larger turbine units could become more attractive as the campus expands.

“We’re leaning towards a rich-burn reciprocating engine for the initial blocks, just because the rich-burn engines accommodate the different fuels better than the lean burns,” Mirick said.

The final generation fleet will depend on the tenant’s reliability requirements and data center design.

Mirick said an initial reciprocating-engine configuration could require about 30% more installed generation than the underlying facility load to provide redundancy.

At a preliminary PUE assumption of 1.3, a 1.5 GW IT load would produce roughly 1.95 GW of facility demand. Applying the illustrative 30% overbuild would put potential installed generation at about 2.5 GW.

That is not a final project design. Prometheus has not disclosed the final generation configuration or installed capacity for Phase 1.

The company expects to use best available control technology and obtain the required air permits for the generation facilities, Mirick said.

## The 2027 Test

The first power target depends on more than the generation equipment. A customer seeking 2027 compute would need to accept modular data center construction, according to Mirick. A conventional custom-built facility would take longer.

“Stick-built, custom design, it’s not possible in our view in 2027,” Mirick said. “You’re probably looking at middle of 2028 at this point.”

Modular construction would allow Prometheus to bring smaller blocks online as equipment arrives, rather than waiting for an entire conventional data hall to be built.

A customer commitment would also trigger orders for the modular data centers and generation equipment, firm gas transportation and project financing.

“The tenant commitment is really the magic that unlocks the capital and gets everything moving,” Mirick said.

Prometheus has not signed a binding customer agreement for a Pecos tenant. Mirick said there is strong early interest but declined to characterize the discussions beyond that.

## Natural Gas First

The Reeves County project’s planned fuel system is designed around pipeline natural gas, with ethane providing additional fuel flexibility.

Istmo Energy’s co-located fractionation facility is under construction, and is expected to enter service in the first quarter of 2028. Until then, the data center’s planned generation would run on pipeline natural gas.

Once the fractionation facility is operating, Prometheus expects a baseline of 85% natural gas and 15% ethane.

Fractionation separates components of a mixed natural gas liquids stream, allowing Istmo to recover ethane for use by the adjacent power system.

“Once you get into ’28 and you’ve got the fractionation, then you’re going to have the ethane backup,” Mirick said.

The precise operating profile of the fuel mix remains dependent on the final generation design. Prometheus also expects on-site ethane storage and, potentially, propane storage.

The company plans two separate methane pipeline connections and firm transportation. If one fuel supply is interrupted, the generators could operate on the other.

“Our base case is 85/15,” Mirick said. “If there’s something wrong with methane pipelines, our checkdown is go full ethane. If there’s something wrong with ethane, you go full methane.”

## What Islanding Changes

Located in Reeves County, the Pecos data center will initially have no physical connection to the ERCOT grid, Mirick said.

“We’re building an island because the island is what allows us to deliver the speed, the reliability that’s required,” he said.

The strategy is a direct response to uncertainty around Texas’ large-load interconnection process. It does not, however, put the project outside Texas regulation. The generation facilities will still require environmental permits and fuel infrastructure, while the project must secure financing and construct a power system capable of operating continuously.

Prometheus could eventually connect the campus to the grid, but Mirick said that would be driven by the tenant.

“We’re not against being grid-connected in the future, but it has to make sense, and it’ll be tenant-directed,” he said.

For now, the company is focused on operating independently of ERCOT.

“We are solely focused on hitting the timetables and reliability metrics through islanding,” Mirick said.

## Taking On Utility-Like Risks

The harder question is whether private generation can deliver hyperscale reliability without simply moving the risks elsewhere. Prometheus expects to use N+1 generation for the initial reciprocating-engine fleet, with the amount of redundancy determined by the customer’s reliability requirements.

“We’re letting them define the number of nines that they want,” Mirick said.

Higher reliability requirements require more generation and electrical infrastructure, he said.

“The more nines, it’s not a linear cost,” Mirick said. “It starts to go up in nonlinear fashion.”

Joshua D. Rhodes, a research scientist at the University of Texas at Austin and a non-resident fellow at Columbia University, said operating generation continuously creates mechanical challenges that are different from the traditional role of standby generators.

“One of the things we’ve seen with running what used to be back up generation full-time is that it increases mechanical stress, and the systems can wear out two to three times as fast,” Rhodes said.

Rhodes said battery storage could serve as a buffer between volatile AI loads and onsite generation, reducing mechanical stress on the engines.

The model shifts more of the operational and commercial risk associated with power infrastructure into the developer-customer relationship.

Prometheus and its eventual customer will have to allocate responsibility for the generation fleet, fuel system and electrical infrastructure that a grid-connected data center would ordinarily obtain through a utility and broader power-supply ecosystem.

## The Cost of Going It Alone

Prometheus also sees private generation as a way to give customers greater certainty over long-term electricity costs.

Mirick estimated the cost of islanded generation at roughly $100 to $125 per megawatt-hour, assuming $3.50/MMBtu for natural gas.

The company did not provide a detailed breakdown of that estimate, including the treatment of generation capital costs, financing, fuel transportation, emissions controls, maintenance and redundancy. It is therefore not a direct comparison with a utility tariff.

“Putting in behind-the-meter, you know what your capex is going to be for power,” Mirick said. “You know what your rate’s going to be for power for 15 years.”

The trade-off is greater responsibility for the infrastructure supplying that power.

“Grid is easy,” Mirick said. “You basically toss the problems over the fence to the utility.”

## Little Water, More Power Infrastructure

The Pecos campus will use closed-loop cooling rather than evaporative cooling.

Mirick said the cooling system would initially contain about 75% water and 25% food-grade propylene glycol. The loop would be filled initially, with limited makeup water expected during normal operation.

Prometheus does not yet have a final design and cannot provide a firm water-consumption figure. Mirick estimated that combined water use for the power and data hall operations could be below the equivalent of roughly 100 households, but said that estimate is preliminary.

The company does not expect the campus to discharge any water during normal operations.

## The Real Test

Pecos is part of Prometheus’ broader strategy of developing data centers around dedicated power systems rather than relying on conventional utility service. The company is also pursuing a Dallas-area project targeting 2027 compute and Wyoming projects targeting 2028.

The strategy can remove one major variable from a data center development schedule: the initial grid interconnection.

But it replaces that variable with a much larger set of responsibilities.

Whether Pecos reaches even its initial 100 MW to 150 MW target in 2027 will depend not on an ERCOT interconnection date, but on whether Prometheus can secure a tenant and prove it can build, fuel, permit, finance and continuously operate its own utility-scale power system.

stories.title: AEMO: Australia's data centres to use 34TWh by 2035-36
stories.summary: The Australian Energy Market Operator projects national data centre electricity consumption will climb from roughly 5TWh today to 34TWh by 2035-36, according to its 2026 Electricity Statement of Opportunities. The forecast implies data centres will take a materially larger share of Australia's total power demand over the next decade.
stories.why_it_matters: AEMO's projection raises the stakes for grid planning, generation investment, and connection approvals in Sydney, Melbourne, and other data centre hubs. Developers face tougher scrutiny over power availability and may need to secure their own generation or storage, while policymakers come under pressure to balance AI growth with grid reliability and household energy costs.
stories.content:
Australia’s data centre sector is set to become a significantly larger consumer of electricity over the next decade, with the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) forecasting annual consumption to rise from around 5TWh today to 34TWh by 2035-36.

The forecast, contained in AEMO’s **2026 Electricity Statement of Opportunities (ESOO)**, would see data centres increase their share of National Electricity Market (NEM) operational consumption from around 3% today to 13% within a decade. AEMO has for the first time **included additional data centre analysis** alongside the ESOO, reflecting the sector’s increasingly significant role in demand forecasting and power-system planning.

AEMO chief executive Daniel Westerman (*above*) said the digital economy was becoming a core part of Australia’s future energy requirements. The 2026 ESOO estimates that around 165 data centres currently consume approximately 5TWh of electricity a year. Average monthly data centre demand across the NEM has risen from almost 200MW in 2018 to more than 700MW in June 2026.

New South Wales currently accounts for 66% of data centre consumption, followed by Victoria at 30%, with South Australia at 2%, Queensland at 1% and Tasmania below 1%. Western Australia sits outside the NEM.

### 67GW pipeline, but significant attrition

The scale of the development pipeline is considerably larger than the forecast consumption growth. Network service providers reported 225 data centre projects at various stages of the connection process for the 2026 ESOO, with combined proposed connection capacity of 67GW, up from 38GW in last year’s assessment. However, AEMO cautions against treating that figure as a forecast of future demand.

Around 36% of the projects included in the 2025 ESOO project list have subsequently been cancelled, including more than 30% of projects previously classified as committed. AEMO says the most advanced developments are concentrated in NSW and Victoria, while projects in South Australia and Tasmania are generally less mature.

AEMO has incorporated that uncertainty into its forecasting methodology, applying probability weightings to individual projects based on factors including project and connection status and developer size. It then combines the resulting project-level forecast with an economic forecast that considers broader digitalisation, AI adoption and Australia’s potential role as an Asia-Pacific data centre hub.

The forecasting methodology also assumes data centres take time to reach full utilisation. AEMO says operators commonly indicate a five-to-10-year period to reach capacity. Current operating data centres remain well below that level, averaging around 27% utilisation in FY26, but AEMO projects that a mature fleet, allowing for planned capacity redundancy and diversified compute profiles, will average 45-51% utilisation depending on data centre type.

### 34TWh central forecast, 52TWh high-growth case

Under AEMO’s Step Change scenario, data centre consumption is forecast to triple to around 15TWh by 2029-30, representing 7.8% of NEM operational consumption, before reaching around 34TWh, or 13%, by 2035-36. But AEMO has also tested a higher-growth scenario to examine what would happen if data centre demand develops more rapidly than assumed in its central forecast.

Under the High Data Centre Growth sensitivity, annual consumption reaches around 52TWh by 2035-36, which is 18TWh, or 56%, above the Step Change forecast. AEMO says the additional growth is concentrated particularly from the early 2030s.

The sensitivity is significant because AEMO has kept the supply-side assumptions unchanged. In other words, it is testing what happens to reliability if data centre demand grows faster without automatically assuming that additional generation, storage and transmission will arrive alongside it.

The result is a substantially tighter reliability outlook. In the high-growth case, expected unserved energy in 2035-36 rises to 5.58% in NSW, 3.95% in Victoria, 2.10% in South Australia and 1.71% in Tasmania, compared with 2.24%, 1.82%, 0.81% and 0.31% respectively under the Government Schemes and Actionable Developments assessment. Queensland is largely unaffected in the sensitivity because data centres currently account for relatively little of its forecast demand growth.

AEMO says that if the higher level of data centre growth assumed for 2035-36 were instead reached four years earlier, in 2031-32, additional investment in generation, storage and transmission would be required from 2032-33 in NSW, Victoria and South Australia to maintain comparable reliability outcomes.

### Supply will need to keep pace

The data centre analysis comes against a broader warning from AEMO that the reliability outlook depends heavily on new generation and storage projects actually being delivered. Under the ESOO’s Government Schemes and Actionable Developments assessment, reliability is maintained within the relevant standard until 2033-34 in NSW, Victoria and South Australia and 2034-35 in Tasmania.

However, when AEMO restricts the assessment to projects that meet its more stringent committed and anticipated development criteria, reliability gaps emerge earlier: from 2030-31 in NSW and Victoria, 2031-32 in South Australia, 2032-33 in Queensland and 2033-34 in Tasmania. The distinction is important for data centre developers because the sector is competing for the same generation, storage and network investment required to replace retiring coal generation and accommodate broader electrification.

AEMO says data centre growth is now a key driver of electricity consumption particularly in NSW, Victoria and South Australia. Its high-growth analysis concludes that timely investment in generation, storage and supporting transmission will be required if demand develops faster than the central forecast.

### Data centres’ role in managing demand

AEMO also identifies a potential opportunity for data centres to provide more flexibility than before from the sector. Greater demand flexibility during periods of supply scarcity could materially reduce the investment required in the electricity system, AEMO says, adding that data centres “may provide greater load flexibility than has been historically observed across existing facilities.”

That could become increasingly relevant as policymakers consider how large new electricity users should integrate with the NEM.

AEMO notes the federal government’s proposed requirements for future large data centres to underwrite their own power supply, as well as the Australian Energy Market Commission’s (AEMC) July 2026 advice to the Energy and Climate Change Ministerial Council, which recommended driving new renewables through the Renewable Electricity Guarantee of Origin scheme, introducing a data centre contracting obligation, introducing market registration requirements, and supporting demand flexibility and co-location with generation through connection agreements.

AEMO has not explicitly modelled the effect of those proposed requirements because it cannot identify which specific generation or storage projects data centre developers might ultimately contract with. It says, however, that if the proposed framework is implemented, some of the additional supply investment needed to support higher data centre growth could be delivered directly by the developers, reducing supply scarcity risks for other consumers.

As a result, the 2026 ESOO therefore presents data centres as both a major new source of electricity demand and a factor that needs to be incorporated more explicitly into system planning. While the central forecast points to a substantial increase in consumption, AEMO’s treatment of the 67GW project pipeline also highlights the gap between proposed capacity and demand that is ultimately likely to materialise.

stories.title: Alibaba Raising $10.2B for AI Infrastructure as Data Centre Push Accelerates
stories.summary: Alibaba Group plans to raise HK$80 billion (US$10.2 billion) by placing 710 million new shares, directing the proceeds toward expanding its AI capabilities and data centre footprint. The placement ranks among the largest equity raises by a Chinese tech company this year and underscores the capital intensity of Alibaba's cloud and AI strategy.
stories.why_it_matters: The raise signals that China's hyperscalers are willing to dilute shareholders to fund AI infrastructure at a pace rivaling US peers, meaning fresh demand for servers, power, and construction capacity across Chinese and regional data centre markets. Investors, equipment suppliers, and competing cloud operators should expect intensified competition for sites and hardware in the region.
stories.content:
Alibaba Cloud took over GLP’s Changshu Southeast Data Centre in Jiangsu province last year (Image: GLP)

Alibaba Group is raising HK$80 billion ($10.2 billion) through a placement of 710 million new shares, with the proceeds earmarked for improvements to its artificial intelligence capabilities, including the expansion and enhancement of data centres, the Chinese e-commerce giant said Monday.

The NYSE- and Hong Kong-listed group priced the shares at HK$112.70 each, generating expected net proceeds of HK$79.7 billion after fees and expenses, according to a filing. The placement is scheduled to close Wednesday.

The new stock represents 3.7 percent of Alibaba’s existing share capital and 3.6 percent of the enlarged total. The issuance adds firepower to Alibaba’s three-year commitment to invest RMB 380 billion ($56.5 billion) in cloud computing and AI infrastructure, with CEO Eddie Wu saying on last week’s fiscal Q1 earnings call that the company had spent RMB 190 billion of that amount by the end of June.

“We delivered a strong quarter, driven by the improving commercialisation of our full-stack AI capabilities,” Wu said in the earnings release. “Alibaba Cloud’s external revenue growth accelerated to 45 percent, with AI-related product revenue delivering triple-digit growth for the 12th consecutive quarter.”

### Investors Drive Stock Down

The latest fundraising ranks as the largest-ever primary follow-on offering by a Hong Kong-listed company and the third largest globally this year, according to data cited by Reuters. Alibaba shares fell nearly 8 percent in HKEX trading after the placement was announced.

Alibaba Group CEO Eddie Wu (Image: Alibaba)

Hangzhou-based Alibaba’s capital expenditure reached RMB 67.7 billion in the three months to June — almost matching the gross proceeds of the share placement and rising 75 percent from the year-earlier period, the company said in the quarterly results.

The increase reflected investment in AI infrastructure to meet customer demand, as well as the addition of computing capacity in anticipation of greater adoption of AI agents and higher prices for a broad range of chip components, Alibaba said.

For the full year to the end of March, capital expenditure jumped 47 percent to RMB 126.1 billion, with the outlays primarily covering computer gear and data centre construction for the group’s cloud business. Contracted capital commitments rose to RMB 54.1 billion from RMB 45.3 billion a year earlier.

The spending pushed free cash flow to a RMB 44.7 billion outflow in the June quarter, widening from an RMB 18.8 billion deficit a year earlier. For the full financial year, free cash flow swung to a RMB 46.6 billion outflow from a RMB 73.9 billion inflow as cloud infrastructure and other spending accelerated.

Group revenue rose 9 percent year-on-year to RMB 269 billion in the June quarter, but adjusted earnings before interest, tax and amortisation fell 30 percent to RMB 27.3 billion and net income dipped 75 percent to RMB 10.4 billion.

In a Substack post, fund manager Michael Burry, who gained fame from predicting the US housing market crash in 2008, said the share issuance fundamentally changed his view of Alibaba.

“I moved my entire Alibaba position into JD not too long ago,” Burry said. “This greatly increased my JD position. I planned to move most of it back after a month or two. No longer.” He added: “I cannot bless share issuances. This is a new paradigm again for BABA, and its ROIC will continue to fall.”

### Debt Already Climbing

The placement is not Alibaba’s first stop at capital markets in the past year.

In September 2025, the company raised $3.2 billion through zero-coupon convertible senior notes due 2032, according to the placing announcement. It had spent all but $518 million of that cash by the end of March. The notes were Alibaba’s only equity-linked issuance in the 12 months before the placement, the filing states.

Debt has climbed alongside capital expenditures, with Alibaba’s total debt standing at 2.29 times adjusted EBITDA as of 31 March. That is roughly double the 1.14 ratio a year earlier, according to the company’s fiscal year 2026 annual report.

Alibaba also issued zero-coupon exchangeable bonds tied to shares of its Alibaba Health subsidiary in July 2025, raising HK$12 billion. Alibaba said the proceeds would help fund its cloud infrastructure buildout.

The company has also pulled back sharply on buybacks in recent months. Alibaba repurchased $1 billion in shares in the fiscal year to the end of March 2026. That is down 91 percent from the $12.8 billion in buybacks in the preceding 12 months, per Mingtiandi calculations based on Alibaba’s annual report.

### Cloud Powers Ahead

Revenue at Alibaba’s newly configured AI cloud and compute services unit surged 45 percent to RMB 48.4 billion in the June quarter, with external sales growing at the same pace.

Adjusted EBITA at the division more than doubled to RMB 5.6 billion, lifting its margin to 12 percent from 7 percent a year earlier. Alibaba cited Omdia research showing that the group led China’s AI cloud market with a 38.1 percent share in 2025.

Alibaba Cloud last week opened its third data centre in South Korea, expanding its global network to 104 availability zones across 30 regions. The company has also been adding capacity in markets including Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, France and the Netherlands.

The hyperscaler’s growth is providing a boost to third-party infrastructure developers, with GLP’s China data centre revenue rising 32 percent in 2025 as the industrial specialist delivered more than 420 megawatts of IT capacity. GLP completed and handed over two facilities to Alibaba Cloud during the year.

Those projects included the second phase of GLP’s 120MW Changshu Southeast Data Centre in Jiangsu province, bringing the converted logistics campus to full capacity. GLP also upgraded nearly 20,000 square metres (215,278 square feet) at its Dongguan Xiegang facility in Guangdong to meet AI computing requirements, with both campuses now listed as Alibaba Cloud access points.

stories.title: Vocus gets to work on route for Sydney-Melbourne fibre
stories.summary: Appoints engineering construction partner.
stories.content:
## Key points

- Vocus has appointed UGL as development partner to begin detailed route planning for its $500 million Sydney-Melbourne ducted fibre link.
- The project, marketed as the Australian Digital Infrastructure Platform, is scheduled to be operational by 2029 and can accommodate up to 3456 fibre pairs.
- Its ducted design will let Vocus add capacity without further civil works, offering greater resilience against cable cuts.

Vocus is set to start detailed route planning for its new $500 million Sydney-Melbourne ducted fibre link with the appointment of a development partner for the project.

The telco has appointed UGL to conduct surveying, designing, engineering, field validation, stakeholder engagement, project management and cost modelling activities.

Vocus chief technology officer Nikos Katinakis said it was an important step in the project which the company is marketing under the name the Australian Digital Infrastructure Platform (ADIP).

“Selecting [UGL] as our development partner is the start of detailed route design and readiness activities on this route," he said.

“Together, we will plan a network with the capacity, resilience and future flexibility required to meet global standards and support Australia’s long-term digital infrastructure needs."

Scheduled to be operational by 2029, the link can accommodate up to 3456 fibre pairs.

Its ducted design will allow Vocus to add capacity to it without engaging in additional civil works.

Katinkas highlighted the design approach when announcing ADIP in June.

"Ducted long-haul fibre networks are more demanding and costly to build but will allow us to add capacity in the future without breaking ground again or interfering with customers' active networks.

"The approach also offers greater resilience and protection against cable cuts to improve customers’ uptime and service levels,” he said.

At the time, Vocus chief executive Andres Irlando said that, despite a flurry of recently announced fibre infrastructure builds, Australia is currently underserved for cable capacity to meet current and future demand for AI.

The carrier has previously told *iTnews* that project ADIP will target areas with land, water and power suitable for AI data centres.
